For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

=== key 1d7e6a8e9b08
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect
Problem: How to sample the largest scaling-experiment training set when some sources (e.g. Gloom) have too few samples for equal stratification.
Write-up text before the decision: K2.6 | MoE | 1T | 32B | 32K | ### I.3 Scaling dataset size experiment In this section, we give the full training protocol for the SFT data-scaling experiment summarized in §4. We measure how monitor quality varies with training-set size $N$ across all model families on six values of $N$. We design the experiment to separate data-quantity effects from training-compute effects. ##### Stratified nested sub-sampling The base training set is the merged corpus with all datasets, specifically STRIDE, Gloom, CoT-Red-Handed, BashArena and BashBench containing $N_{\max}{=}8688$ structured rationale training with equal numbers of benign and misaligned trajectories per source. Sub-samples of size $N\in\{204,504,996,2004,4008,8688\}$ are drawn under two constraints: 1. Stratification by source $\times$ class. Each $N$ has $N/12$ examples from every (source, ground-truth) pair, so all five upstream datasets and both classes are represented in equal proportion at every scale. The sizes were chosen to be exactly divisible by $12$ for this reason; the smallest size $N{=}204$ yields $17$ examples per stratum. 2. Nested prefixes. Sub-sample $N_{i}\subset N_{i+1}$ for every $i$, so any larger run sees a strict superset of the smaller run’s data. We achieve this by drawing one permutation per stratum and taking prefixes of length $N/12$ from each. The largest scale $N{=}8688$ follows the nested prefixing, but uses the full available pool of samples, and hence is the only exception to stratified sampling by source. This is owing to datasets such as Gloom having only 386 samples per class.
